Significance We have experimentally investigated the immunoregulatory effects of human gut microbiota in multiple sclerosis (MS). We have identified specific bacteria that are associated with MS and demonstrated that these bacteria regulate T lymphocyte-mediated adaptive immune responses and contribute to the proinflammatory environment in vitro and in vivo. Thus, our results expand the knowledge of the microbial regulation of immunity and may provide a basis for the development of microbiome-based therapeutics in autoimmune diseases. Keywords: multiple sclerosis, microbiome, autoimmunity Abstract The gut microbiota regulates T cell functions throughout the body. We hypothesized that intestinal bacteria impact the pathogenesis of multiple sclerosis (MS), an autoimmune disorder of the CNS and thus analyzed the microbiomes of 71 MS patients not undergoing treatment and 71 healthy controls. Although no major shifts in microbial community structure were found, we identified specific bacterial taxa that were significantly associated with MS. Akkermansia muciniphila and Acinetobacter calcoaceticus , both increased in MS patients, induced proinflammatory responses in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells and in monocolonized mice. In contrast, Parabacteroides distasonis , which was reduced in MS patients, stimulated antiinflammatory IL-10–expressing human CD4 CD25 T cells and IL-10 FoxP3 Tregs in mice. Finally, microbiota transplants from MS patients into germ-free mice resulted in more severe symptoms of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis and reduced proportions of IL-10 Tregs compared with mice “humanized” with microbiota from healthy controls. This study identifies specific human gut bacteria that regulate adaptive autoimmune responses, suggesting therapeutic targeting of the microbiota as a treatment for MS. A major role of the human gut microbiota is to regulate both innate and adaptive immune responses during health and disease ( 1 ). Most studies of the human microbiome to date have focused on analyzing microbial population structures. However, it is equally important to investigate how variability in microbial abundance and composition affects host functions ( 2 , 3 ). Exposing primary human immune cells to microbes or microbial products in vitro allows functional investigation of immunomodulatory effects by the gut microbiota ( 4 – 6 ). There is growing evidence of population differences in the gut microbiota in multiple human autoimmune diseases ( 7 , 8 ), including multiple sclerosis (MS) ( 9 – 12 ). While these studies in MS were performed with small sample sizes and did not stratify patient groups by treatment with disease-modifying drugs, consistent patterns of modest dysbiosis appear to be emerging. Furthermore, microbiota have been shown to mediate the regulation of immune responses in experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), a mouse model of MS ( 13 , 14 ). MS-like symptoms in EAE can be exacerbated by Th1 and Th17 responses and modulated by Tregs ( 15 , 16 ). This led us to investigate structural and functional changes in intestinal microbiota as a potential component of MS pathogenesis. Specifically, we identified differences in microbial abundance between MS patients and controls and investigated how particular MS-associated bacteria modulate T lymphocyte responses using both in vitro and in vivo model systems. Our results indicate that differences in specific gut bacteria are functionally associated with a shift toward a proinflammatory T cell profile that may exacerbate or perpetuate autoimmune responses, thus potentially identifying a previously unknown environmental contributor to MS pathogenesis. Results The MS Microbiome Elicits Differential Treg Responses and Shows Modest Dysbiosis at the Genus Level. To investigate whether MS-associated bacteria affect immune functions in the host, we stimulated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from MS patients or healthy controls, using extracts from total bacteria isolated from the stool samples of the same subjects who were PBMC donors (thus, “self” bacterial extracts). We observed that PBMCs from MS patients showed an impaired ability to differentiate or expand CD25 FoxP3 Treg populations ( Fig. 1 A ). The total CD3 CD4 Th lymphocyte population was not altered by bacterial extract treatment, and the baseline proportion of CD25 FoxP3 Tregs (in a population of CD3 CD4 T cells) was not different between MS patients and healthy controls. These results suggest a specific immunoregulatory role of microbiota on PBMCs from MS patients. We subsequently analyzed the microbiome by 16S rRNA gene sequencing of stool samples from 71 untreated relapsing–remitting MS patients and 71 healthy controls ( SI Appendix , Table S1 ). A subset of 79 subjects was sampled on two consecutive days to account for variability over time, and all subjects were used to compare the variability within and between subject groups ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 ). Consistent with similar findings in other autoimmune diseases ( 7 , 8 ), we did not observe major global shifts in bacterial community structure in terms of alpha or beta diversity ( Fig. 1 B and C ). However, significant differences at the level of individual microbial taxa were observed between MS and control subjects ( Figs. 1 D and 2 ). Our analysis revealed significant differences in the relative abundance of 25 bacterial genera (19.38% of the total) (listed in SI Appendix , Table S2 ) and 247 operational taxonomic units (OTUs) (16.89% of the total) (listed in SI Appendix , Table S3 ) ( Fig. 2 A and B ). We then selected individual significantly different taxa for functional studies to assess their potential contribution to autoimmune inflammation in MS. The specific taxa were selected based on the following criteria: ( i ) identifiable to species level or genus level with high overlap between species; ( ii ) culturable, to be able to study their functions in vitro and in vivo; ( iii ) type strains available from the ATCC to ensure reproducibility; and ( iv ) previously associated with immunoregulatory effects. Among the genera significantly increased in MS samples were Acinetobacter and Akkermansia , while one of the most significantly reduced genera in MS patients was Parabacteroides , with the majority of OTUs mapping to Parabacteroides distasonis ( Fig. 2 C and SI Appendix , Fig. S3 ). Interestingly, P . distasonis was previously reported to induce a Treg phenotype in gnotobiotic mouse models ( 17 , 18 ). All Acinetobacter species, including Acinetobacter baumannii , Acinetobacter calcoaceticus , and Acinetobacter lwoffii , are rare in the healthy human gut microbiome and share genome-wide homology ( 19 , 20 ), making them indistinguishable by 16S amplicon sequencing. Thus, OTUs that mapped to the genus Acinetobacter did not allow species-level discrimination. Based on a previous report associating A . calcoaceticus with MS ( 21 ), we focused on this organism as a candidate for functional studies of immune regulation. Finally, all OTUs that mapped to the Akkermansia genus belonged to the species Akkermansia muciniphila , which has been studied mostly in the context of metabolism ( 22 ) but also contributes to inflammation during infection ( 12 , 23 ). MS-Associated Bacterial Species Reduce Tregs and Increase Th1 Lymphocyte Differentiation in Vitro. We hypothesized that bacterial taxa altered in MS patients play functional roles in regulating immune responses. To test this hypothesis, we established an in vitro model system by exposing PBMCs from healthy donors to a suspension of heat-killed and sonicated individual bacterial cultures (“bacterial extracts”) under different stimulating conditions (e.g., Treg, Th1, and so forth) and used flow cytometry to evaluate T lymphocyte differentiation and proliferation. We observed that extracts from A . calcoaceticus reduced the proportions of CD25 FoxP3 Tregs among PBMCs ( Fig. 3 A and B ). These results suggest that intestinal A . calcoaceticus restrains immunoregulatory T cell development, as is consistent with its relative increase in the MS cohort. Furthermore, we observed that A . calcoaceticus increased the proportion of effector CD4 lymphocytes that differentiated into IFNγ-producing Th1 cells ( Fig. 3 C and D ), thereby potentially exacerbating inflammation. Analysis of A . muciniphila , another bacterial species increased in the MS microbiome, revealed an even more pronounced effect on stimulating Th1 differentiation. Extracts from A . muciniphila significantly increased healthy donor PBMC differentiation into Th1 lymphocytes ( Fig. 4 A – D ). Furthermore, we discovered that the mere presence of A . muciniphila in total stool bacteria was sufficient to increase Th1 lymphocyte differentiation in vitro. Specifically, exposing PBMCs to total bacterial extracts isolated from unrelated subjects with detectable levels of A . muciniphila increased the differentiation of IFNγ Th1 lymphocytes compared with bacterial extracts that did not have A . muciniphila ( Fig. 4 E and G ). Similarly, subjects with detectable A . muciniphila showed a significant increase in IFNγ Th1 differentiation in response to extracts of their own bacteria ( Fig. 4 F and H ). In summary, we have identified A . muciniphila and A . calcoaceticus as examples of common and rare MS-associated bacterial species that favor proinflammatory T lymphocyte responses in vitro. We next explored whether individual taxa that are less abundant in MS patients could promote immunoregulatory responses. Exposing healthy donor PBMCs to extracts from P . distasonis significantly increased the percentage of CD25 T lymphocytes among the CD3 CD4 T cell population ( Fig. 5 A and B ). Furthermore, we observed an enrichment of CD25 IL-10 cells ( Fig. 5 C and D ), including CD25 IL-10 FoxP3 Tr1 cells (but not CD25 FoxP3 Tregs), which have been associated with strong immunoregulatory properties ( 14 , 24 ). Thus, our results demonstrate that P . distasonis is sufficient to skew T lymphocytes toward a regulatory profile in vitro. All immunoregulatory effects described here were at least partially specific to selected bacterial extracts. To show that exposure to any differentially abundant bacteria did not elicit similar effects, we analyzed the immune effects of Eggerthella lenta , which is significantly increased in MS patients, and found that it did not alter Th1 or Treg differentiation ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3 A and B ). In addition, the specificity of P . distasonis , A . calcoaceticus , and A . muciniphila functions is emphasized by the fact that these bacteria did not alter the differentiation of all lymphocyte populations indiscriminately; for example, P . distasonis had no effect on Th1 cells, and A . muciniphila had no effect on CD25 FoxP3 Tregs ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3 C – E ). While regulation of immune functions by gut microbiota are likely multifaceted and complex, we speculate that the observed P . distasonis- associated reduction in immunoregulatory T cells could act in concert with the described increases in A . calcoaceticus and A . muciniphila and contribute to create an overall proinflammatory environment in MS patients. Colonization of Mice with Single Species of MS-Associated Bacteria Recapitulates in Vitro T Lymphocyte Differentiation Profiles. To elucidate the role of individual MS-associated bacteria in vivo, we colonized antibiotic-treated or germ-free (GF) mice with a single species: A . calcoaceticus , A . muciniphila , or P . distasonis . Following colonization, we measured T lymphocyte differentiation in multiple peripheral lymphoid tissues. We were unable to observe an effect of A . muciniphila in monocolonized mice as described in our in vitro experiments, and we hypothesize that this discrepancy is likely due to differences in host (e.g., mice vs. human). However, we were able to replicate our key findings with the other two species analyzed. In antibiotic-treated mice A . calcoaceticus inhibited FoxP3 Treg differentiation, while P . distasonis stimulated CD4 IL-10 lymphocyte differentiation ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 A and B ). Furthermore, splenocytes from mice colonized with P . distasonis also displayed induction of CD4 IL10 lymphocytes in response to their bacterial extracts, while this was not observed when splenocytes from control SPF mice were exposed to their own bacterial extracts ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 C ). Furthermore, monocolonization of GF mice with A . calcoaceticus increased T lymphocyte differentiation into the IFNγ Th1 phenotype in cervical lymph nodes ( Fig. 6 A and B ), while monocolonization with P . distasonis led to significant increases in the CD4 IL-10 T lymphocyte population in mesenteric lymph nodes and spleens ( Fig. 6 C and SI Appendix , Fig. S5 ). Taken together, the in vivo monocolonization results form a consistent complement to our in vitro data. Colonization of Mice with MS Donor Microbiota Inhibits Treg Differentiation and Exacerbates Disease Severity in EAE. To investigate whether the proinflammatory environment established by MS-associated bacteria is physiologically relevant, we randomly selected three MS and control donor pairs (each composed of an untreated relapsing–remitting MS patient and a household control) to perform fecal microbiota transplants into groups of GF C57BL/6 mice ( n = 6–8 mice per group). Six weeks after transplantation, mice were immunized with myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG 35–55 ) to induce EAE. Remarkably, EAE disease scores were significantly increased in mice colonized with microbiota from MS patients compared with animals colonized with microbiota from healthy controls or GF mice ( Fig. 7 A ). This result was recapitulated across all three donor pairs tested ( SI Appendix , Fig. S6 ) and was accompanied by a lack of IL-10 Treg induction in mesenteric lymph nodes from MS microbiota-colonized mice ( Fig. 7 C – F and SI Appendix , Fig. S7 ). RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) was performed on spinal cord samples derived from GF mice humanized with MS ( n = 11) or control ( n = 9) microbiota before and after EAE induction. Analysis of transcripts with differential expression in the two groups before and after EAE identified the up-regulation of several genes identified as the “immune response gene” category. Interestingly, when this dataset was used to infer the enrichment of specific cell types in the CNS, we detected a noticeable enrichment toward genes expressed by microglia in mice colonized with MS microbiota compared with controls ( SI Appendix , Fig. S8 ). The inability of fecal bacteria from MS patients to promote Treg responses was observed both pre- and post-EAE induction, consistent with the microbiota showing no major differences in beta diversity at time points before and after the disease ( Fig. 7 B ). Principal component analysis of beta diversity of the microbiota in recipient animals showed a significant separation by donor that was stabilized as early as 7 d after transplantation ( Fig. 7 B and SI Appendix , Fig. S9 A ). This separation was recapitulated by metrics of alpha diversity ( SI Appendix , Fig. S9 B ). Interestingly, some of the changes in relative abundance of individual bacterial genera, including a decrease in Sutterella and an increase in Ruminococcus , were also observed in mice colonized with microbiota from MS-discordant twins ( SI Appendix , Fig. S9 C ) ( 25 ). Although human and mouse microbiota are not directly comparable, the biological pathways represented by MS-associated taxa largely overlap in the two groups ( SI Appendix , Tables S3 and S4 ). Collectively, the MS microbial community in vivo enhances EAE disease progression and fails to induce IL-10 Tregs relative to gut bacteria from healthy controls, suggesting a functional role for the microbiota in autoimmunity that may be independent of host factors. Discussion Here we present a comparative structural analysis of the gut microbiome from patients with MS followed by functional studies of MS-associated microbiota. Our results reinforce the concept of MS pathogenesis as a multihit model that combines genetic predisposition and environmental factors, one of which is the microbiota. Based on our findings, we hypothesize that gut microbiota contribute to creating a sustained proinflammatory environment, which, in combination with genetic and other environmental factors, may crystallize the pathogenic autodestructive process of myelin. In our admittedly simplistic experimental setup, we used crude bacterial extracts without prior fractionation; thus the relevant active components may consist of any bacterial products, either secreted or intracellular. Known bacterial metabolites with immunoregulatory effects fall into multiple categories, including polysaccharides ( 26 ), short-chain fatty acids ( 27 ), and aryl hydrocarbons ( 28 ). In addition, although we analyzed the effects of bacterial extracts on peripheral immune cells, some bacterial metabolites are able to cross the blood–CNS barrier and directly regulate CNS inflammation via microglia ( 29 , 30 ) or astrocytes ( 28 ). Future research will likely be directed toward identifying the therapeutic potential of such products in MS and other complex diseases. Although intestinal A . muciniphila has been extensively studied in the context of diet and obesity ( 22 , 31 ), its role in regulating immune responses is less well understood. Here we provide in vitro evidence that A . muciniphila promotes Th1 lymphocyte differentiation. Consistent with our observations, A . muciniphila has been reported to exacerbate inflammation during infection ( 23 ). In contrast, a recent study reported that EAE-resistant male TNFR2 mice harbor more A . muciniphila than do disease-susceptible TNFR2 females ( 32 ). However, it remains to be addressed whether EAE susceptibility in this genotype is driven by the gut microbiome or by other factors that stem from gender and genetic differences. Notably, in a recently published study ( 12 ), as well as in companion the MS-discordant twin study in this issue of PNAS ( 25 ), Akkermansia was reported to be elevated in untreated MS patients. The higher prevalence of Acinetobacter within MS subjects is consistent with previous reports of increased serum antibody responses ( 21 , 33 ). Strikingly, A . calcoaceticus has also been shown to encode peptides that mimic the amino acid sequences of myelin basic protein (MBP) and MOG ( 21 ), both of which are myelin components ( 34 ). This suggests that molecular mimicry could potentially convert a normal immune response toward Acinetobacter into autoimmunity against myelin. Recently, another model of molecular mimicry-mediated CNS autoimmunity was proposed when aquaporin four-specific T lymphocytes from neuromyelitis optica patients were found to recognize a peptide from Clostridium perfringens and induce a Th17 bias ( 6 ), and this organism was found to be overabundant in neuromyelitis optica patients compared with healthy controls ( 35 ). A growing body of literature has associated both CD25 FoxP3 Tregs and IL-10–expressing T lymphocytes with alterations in gut microbiota. For example, monocolonization of GF mice with specific bacterial species is sufficient to drive CD25 FoxP3 Treg differentiation and alter disease phenotype ( 3 ). Of interest, P . distasonis has also been shown to induce Treg differentiation in GF mice ( 2 ). In addition, our findings suggest that in vivo exposure to pure P . distasonis is associated with a subsequent immunoregulatory response to this bacterium in vitro. This observation is supported by the result that the immune cells of MS patients have impaired Treg differentiation in response to autologous (self) bacteria. Thus, the initial exposure to P . distasonis or other “beneficial” bacteria found in healthy subjects may contribute to expanding regulatory T lymphocyte precursor populations, thus promoting antiinflammatory responses upon subsequent exposure to the same bacteria. While previous studies using GF mouse models have identified that the absence of gut bacteria ameliorates EAE ( 13 , 14 ), here we show that gut bacteria transplanted from MS patients promotes more severe EAE symptoms than seen in mice that were transplanted with fecal bacteria from household controls. Similar results of microbiota being sufficient to transfer a human donor phenotype to GF mice have been reported in the context of obesity ( 36 ) and inflammatory bowel disease ( 37 ), and rheumatoid arthritis-associated bacteria were shown to exacerbate the disease in a mouse model of colitis ( 7 ). However, our study shows that the gut microbiota is able to transfer the phenotype in a disease model unrelated to the digestive system and suggests a potentially causal role for the gut microbiota in MS. We consider GF mouse monocolonization as a valid experimental model to study microbial functions in vivo. However, we also recognize this approach has caveats, as monocolonization may not represent bacterial functions within the entire microbial community of the gut, and it requires using a mouse host for bacteria that presumably have a function in human disease. Therefore, it is not surprising to find that in vivo studies using monocolonized mice do not completely replicate in vitro results from human cells. We interpret our in vitro and in vivo findings as the first step toward future studies to identify pathways and metabolites that modulate Th1 and IL-10 regulatory T lymphocytes. Such studies will likely open new avenues for the development of novel, microbiome-based therapeutic approaches for autoimmunity. PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC12047500  PMID: 40185103 Summary Progressive multiple sclerosis (MS) is a neurological disease with limited understanding of the biology associated with transition from relapsing to progressive disease. Intestinal microbes and metabolites are altered in MS, but relation to disease progression is largely unknown. We investigate microbiota and metabolites in subjects with stable MS, those who worsened, and in those with relapsing MS who became progressive over 2 years. We find that Eubacterium hallii , Butyricoccaceae , Blautia , and other short-chain fatty-acid-producing microbes have beneficial associations with worsening of disability, 3T magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measures, cognition, and quality of life, while Alistipes is detrimentally associated. Global metabolomics identified serum and stool metabolites that are altered in progressive MS and in relapsing subjects who transitioned to progressive disease. Most fecal metabolites associated with disease progression are decreased, suggesting a deficiency of protective factors in the gut. Using a unique MS cohort, our findings identify gut microbiome and metabolite pathways influencing progressive MS. Keywords: progressive MS, gut microbiome, metabolomics, MRI, disease progression, fatty acids, microbial metabolites Graphical abstract Highlights • Gut microbes are linked to 2-year changes in MS disability, MRI, and quality of life • Serum and stool metabolites are linked to the development of progressive MS • Subjects who worsened are missing potentially beneficial microbial metabolites Understanding pathobiology at the shift from relapsing to progressive multiple sclerosis (MS) is critically important. In this study, Schwerdtfeger et al. use a 2-year follow-up cohort to show that subjects with MS who became progressive are missing microbes that produce beneficial metabolites. These microbes and metabolites are targets for supplementation in MS. Introduction Multiple studies have identified abnormalities in the gut microbiome in multiple sclerosis (MS). Intestinal microbes and their metabolites are known to influence a wide variety of processes related to both health and disease. In terms of MS, a major question is the manner in which intestinal microbes and their metabolites are related to different stages of the disease and to the development of progressive MS from relapsing remitting forms. Studies in relapsing MS have identified increased Akkermansia muciniphila and decreased butyrate producers. In a cross-sectional study of progressive MS, we identified microbes associated with clinical measurements of disease including disability, brain MRI, and quality of life and found beneficial associations with Akkermansia. A major unanswered question is the degree to which the gut microbiome and its metabolites are associated with both longitudinal changes in clinical and radiological measures of disease severity and in the transition to progressive MS. Microbial metabolites influence health and disease by affecting both immunologic and neural pathways. Serum and stool metabolites are altered in MS, including lipids, fatty acid metabolites, secondary bile acids, and tryptophan derivatives. Several of these metabolites are known to be produced by the gut microbiota, and secondary bile acids are made exclusively by intestinal microbes. Individuals with MS have decreased stool levels of microbially derived metabolites providing a rationale for clinical trials with these metabolites. Disease progression in MS can be measured by change in disease severity, MRI measures, quality of life measures (e.g., fatigue), biomarkers of degeneration, and most importantly by the transition from the relapsing to the progressive form of MS. The Comprehensive Longitudinal Investigation of MS at the Brigham and Women’s Hospital (CLIMB study) comprises a cohort of patients followed longitudinally with regular clinical assessment, MRI, and blood and stool collections, and we have previously demonstrated the utility of fluid biomarkers including neurofilament light and glial fibrillary acidic protein in predicting disease worsening using CLIMB samples. The CLIMB study thus provides a unique opportunity to understand how the gut microbiota and its metabolites are associated with disease progression in MS. Using the CLIMB cohort, we identified microbes and metabolites that decreased in subjects who worsened clinically vs. those who remained stable. In addition, we identified microbes associated with brain MRI measures of disease and quality of life. Our findings identify pathways by which the gut microbiome and its metabolites influence progressive MS. Results Identification of microbiota linked to disease worsening To identify microbes linked to clinical outcomes, we investigated subjects with MS whose expanded disability status scale (EDSS) worsened over a 2-year period, as defined by an increase of ≥1, and compared them to subjects with MS with an EDSS change of ≤1 point or improved ( Figure 1 A). This is an EDSS change routinely defined as the minimally clinically important difference. Subjects with a baseline EDSS between 1.5 and 3.5 and who remained on the same disease-modifying therapy (DMT) during the 2-year follow-up period were selected for analysis. At baseline, there were no differences in EDSS between groups. As expected, there was a significant increase in EDSS in the worsening group ( Figure 1 B; p < 0.0001). Of the subjects who worsened, 20.8% had a relapse during the 2-year follow-up, whereas relapses were observed in 8.2% of subjects without EDSS worsening ( Figure 1 C). Age, BMI ( Figure 1 D), DMT, or the percentage of male vs. female subjects was not different between stable and worsened groups ( Table S1 ), and there was no difference in 2-year EDSS related to DMT ( Figure 1 E). α-diversity metrics including Evenness, Faith’s phylogenetic diversity (PD), Shannon’s index, or richness were not different between EDSS groups ( Figure 1 F). We visualized effect size of potential confounders associated with variation in microbiota via a weighted Adonis R and did not find any significant contribution of these factors on permutational multivariate ANOVA ( Figure 1 G). β-diversity was not altered in stable vs. worsened EDSS groups as measured by weighted and unweighted UniFrac distances ( Figure 1 H). Microbiome multivariable associations with linear models (MaAsLin2) was used to associate microbial amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) with a 2-year change in EDSS controlled for covariates including age, BMI, DMT, and the percentage of male and female subjects. We found four ASVs negatively associated with a 2-year change in EDSS and three ASVs positively associated ( Figure 1 I, p < 0.05). ASVs were initially identified using the SILVA taxonomic database in QIIME2. For further identification, we also used the basic local alignment search tool (BLAST, Table S2 ). We found that Alistipes ( A. onderdonkii , 100% BLAST identity) and 2 Bacteroides ASVs ( B. xylanisolvens , 100% BLAST identity and Phocaeicola vulgatus , 100% BLAST identity) were associated with an increased 2-year change in EDSS and Streptococcus ( S. thermophilus , 100% BLAST identity), Eubacterium hallii ( A. hallii , 100% BLAST identity), Butyricicoccus ( A. butyriciproducens , 100% BLAST identity), and Eggerthella ( E. bacterium , 100% BLAST identity) were associated with a decreased 2-year change in EDSS. Consistent with this, we found that subjects who worsened had decreased Streptococcus ASV -0179bed8fd230300765694433b3858c9 and increased Bacteroides ASV-024a4a4e09775389a6cd47c02a336ddb at baseline ( Figure 1 J). Use of a DMT may shift gut microbiota composition. We investigated the relationship between microbiota in subjects on one of eight common DMTs vs. untreated subjects. We found multiple Blautia genera and Eubacterium hallii elevated in subjects on anti-CD20 therapy compared to untreated subjects. Furthermore, anti-CD20 therapy was negatively associated with Erysipelotrichaceae and Bacteroides dorei ( Figure S1 ). Gut microbes correlate with 2-year changes in 3T MRI Brain atrophy and lesion volume are well-established measures of disease severity in MS. We investigated the association between the microbiota and longitudinal MRI changes. When we compared untreated subjects with those receiving DMTs, we found no differences in changes in total deep gray matter (DGM) volume ( Figure 2 A), whole brain parenchymal volume ( Figure 2 B), and whole brain T2 white matter lesion volume (T2LV; Figure 2 C). In addition, MRI changes were not correlated with a 2-year change in EDSS, age, or BMI ( Figure S2 ). Microbial taxa correlated with changes in seven brain volumetric measures. We found multiple bacteria that correlated with changes in whole brain volume, DGM, thalamus, caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus volumes, including Lachnospiraceae and Alistipes genera members ( Figure 2 D). We also found microbes that correlated with T2LV, including A. onderdonkii and Streptococcus ( Figure 2 E) . T2LV and atrophy represent different disease processes in MS. T2LV represents white matter foci of inflammatory demyelination whereas atrophy is associated with widespread neurodegeneration of gray and white matter. We found unique microbes associated with T2LV or atrophy, suggesting that the microbiome influences T2LV vs. atrophy by different mechanisms. Gut microbes associated with cognitive changes in MS It is well recognized that cognitive changes occur in MS. Cognitive testing was performed in a subset of subjects ( Table S1 ) within 6 months of microbiome sampling, and 2 years later. We investigated subjects whose symbol digit modality test (SDMT) increased, was stable, or decreased ( Figure 3 A), defined as a change of ±4 points as previously described. SDMT outcomes were not associated with age or EDSS ( Figures 3 B and 3C). Three taxa were correlated with worsening of SDMT, including a Ruminococcus gauvreauii group member, Lachnoclostridium , and Eubacterium ( Figure 3 D). Similar to microbes associated with less brain atrophy ( Figure 2 D), a Ruminococcus genus member and a Peptostreptococcaceae member were associated with an improved SDMT score ( Figure 3 D). Another measure of cognition in MS is the California verbal learning test (CVLT-II), which measures speed of language processing. A change in the CVLT-II was defined as an increase or decrease of 3 points over a 2-year period as previously defined ( Figure 3 E). A decreased CVLT-II score was associated with increasing age ( Figure 3 F, p = 0.04; Spearman’s rho = −0.243, p = 0.022), but not with EDSS ( Figure 3 G). We identified microbes that correlated with a 0–2 year worsening on the CVLT-II score, including Clostridium sensu stricto and Turicibacter . We also identified multiple Lachnoclostridium and Bacteroides genera associated with an improvement in CVLT-II, suggesting a beneficial role ( Figure 3 H). Gut microbes associated with quality-of-life changes in MS The Quality of Life in Neurological Disorders (Neuro-QoL) survey assesses health-related quality of life across 11 physical, mental, and social domains. Neuro-QoL domain T scores between subjects with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) and progressive MS (ProgMS) were stable across 0–2 years ( Figure 4 A). Similar to microbes associated with EDSS worsening, A. onderdonkii was negatively correlated with change in the lower extremity function Neuro-QoL domain ( Figure 4 B). Furthermore, there were multiple beneficial associations with Eubacterium hallii including positive correlations with change in upper extremity function, ability to participate in social roles and activities, satisfaction with social roles and activities, and cognitive function ( Figure 4 B). Serum metabolites linked to the development of progressive MS To identify both microbially and host-produced metabolites related to disease progression, we performed global metabolomics on serum and stool. We compared samples from an independent cohort ( Table S3 ) with groups: healthy controls (HCs), subjects with RRMS who remained stable (RR → RR), subjects with RRMS who transitioned to secondary progressive MS (SPMS; RR → SP), and subjects with SPMS who were matched based on age, the percentage of male and female subjects, race/ethnicity, and DMT usage ( Table S3 ). Subjects who transitioned to SPMS (RR → SP) were classified by their clinician’s diagnosis based on continued worsening of neurological exam and increasing EDSS. All diagnoses were independently confirmed by a second MS clinician through chart review. Subjects who transitioned (RR → SP) had higher EDSS at the 2-year follow-up vs. baseline ( Figure 5 A) and longer 25-foot walking times than stable RR → RR subjects ( Figure 5 B). Principal component analysis showed clustering of serum metabolites by disease category and the percentage of male and female subjects ( Figure 5 C). We identified hundreds of metabolites that differed between groups, with the largest group differences detected between ProgMS and HC and the smallest differences detected between the RR → SP and RR → RR groups ( Figure 5 D). To determine if there were metabolites uniquely associated with MS progression, we identified metabolites that were altered in both subjects with RR → SP and SPMS vs. HCs but not in RR → RR vs. HCs. We found an increase in 8 lipids and 1 xenobiotic and a decrease in 6 lipids and 6 xenobiotics ( Figure 5 E). Specifically, we found elevated palmitoleate (16:1n7) and p-cresol sulfate and a decrease in the secondary bile acids iso- and ursodeoxycholate ( Figures 5 E and 5F). Furthermore, we investigated metabolites correlated with a change in EDSS and found 5 metabolites linked with worsening and 26 with stability/improvement, a majority of which were lipids or xenobiotics ( Figure S3 A). We next investigated metabolites linked with a recent transition to progressive MS by comparing RR → RR vs. RR → SP subjects. Volcano plot shows altered metabolites with a log 2 fold change cutoff of ±1 ( Figure 5 G). In total, 27 metabolites were altered in RR → SP compared with RR → RR subjects, with 18 being elevated and 9 decreased in RR → SP based on analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) contrasts ( Figure 5 D). Pathway enrichment score (PES) analysis was performed to identify metabolic pathways associated with the transition to progressive MS. We found 17 pathways that were enriched (PES > 1) in RR → SP subjects, with vitamin B6, fatty acid synthesis, glycerolipid metabolism, and xenobiotic respiratory drugs being the most enriched ( Figure 5 H). Stool metabolites linked to the development of progressive MS We next performed global metabolomics on stool and found that principal component analysis showed clustering of metabolites by disease category and the percentage of male and female subjects ( Figure 6 A). Consistent with our serum metabolomics, the greatest number of differences was found between SPMS and HCs. In addition, SPMS vs. RR → SP subjects had the fewest differences, suggesting a unique metabolomic signature associated with disease progression in MS ( Figure 6 B). We found that metabolites linked to disease progression were decreased vs. HCs ( Figure 6 C), including nicotinate, protoporphyrin IX, phenyllactate, and N1,N12-diacetylspermine ( Figures 6 C and 6D). A total of 85 metabolites were altered in subjects with RR → SP vs. RR → RR MS, with all but 5 being decreased in RR → SP ( Figure 6 E). A majority of these alterations were in amino acids, lipids, nucleotides, or xenobiotics. We identified fecal metabolic pathways that were altered in RR → SP vs. stable RR → RR MS and found an increase in 35 pathways related to sugar metabolism, polypeptides, and purine/pyrimidine metabolism ( Figure 6 F). We next investigated metabolites linked to a change in EDSS and found 7 metabolites correlated with worsening and 65 with stability/improvement, a majority of which were amino acids, lipids, nucleotides, or peptides ( Figure S3 B). To investigate the relationship between serum and stool metabolites, we identified metabolites that were altered in both matrices. The majority of metabolites altered in MS were increased or decreased in both serum and stool. However, multiple lipids that were elevated in serum were decreased in stool including palmitoleate and N-oleoyltaurine ( Figure S4 ). Furthermore, we observed altered secondary bile acids associated with MS worsening in serum ( Figures S5 A and S5B) and stool ( Figures S5 C and S5D). Stool levels of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) including acetate, butyrate, valerate, propionate, isobutyrate, and isovalerate were not associated with disease worsening or DMT status ( Figures S5 E–S5G). Microbiota predicted to produce metabolites linked to MS progression Using MetOrigin analysis, we identified 193 stool metabolites that were derived only from microbiota. We then used the MetOrigin microbiota-predicted metabolite pathway analysis and found that the majority of metabolic pathways were driven by metabolites comprising a combination of host and microbial factors ( Figure 7 A). We next used MMvec to investigate which members of the microbiota were capable of producing stool metabolites that were altered in RR → SP vs. RR → RR subjects ( Figures 6 E and 7 B). We found that stool metabolites, which correlated with the transition to progressive MS, were associated with the production of metabolites including pyridoxamine and nicotinate by Akkermansia , xanthine and erythronate by multiple Lachnospiraceae , and sphingomyelin by Eubacterium hallii ( Figure 7 B). Furthermore, when we investigated all 85 stool metabolites ( Figure S6 ) and a subset of serum metabolites ( Figure S7 ) that were altered in RR → SP vs. RR → RR, we found that similar microbes were implicated in the production of these metabolites. Discussion Although the gut microbiome is altered in RRMS and ProgMS, specific microbes and metabolites associated with disease worsening and the transition to progressive disease have not been identified. Using our longitudinal CLIMB cohort, we investigated subjects who transitioned from RRMS to progressive disease. This provided a unique opportunity to identify microbial metabolic signaling pathways involved in the clinical transition from relapsing to progressive disease, which is the major cause of MS disability. We found microbiota that were associated with changes in EDSS over a 2-year period. Specifically, species from the genera Butyricoccus and Eubacterium hallii were negatively correlated with a 2-year change in EDSS, suggesting a beneficial role. Consistent with other follow-up studies, we found an increase in Bacteroides and a decrease in multiple Lachnospiraceae associated with disease worsening. These genera are producers of SCFAs including butyrate. Nonetheless, we did not observe altered SCFA profiles. In subjects who transitioned from relapsing to progressive MS, multiple Lachnospiraceae family members were decreased. These included Blautia species, microbes that play a regulatory role in the gut. Conversely, two Bacteroides genera and one Alistipes were positively associated with a 2-year change in EDSS, suggesting a role in driving disease worsening. Alistipes has been associated with other CNS diseases including Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s and is associated with an increased risk of colonic cancer and major depression. Of note, Alistipes obesi was reported to be elevated in MS vs. healthy controls in one study, but not in another. Elevated abundance of a microbe can correlate with disease worsening; however, this does not necessitate a detrimental effect. Transferring MS-derived microbiomes to mice can trigger spontaneous experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), and MS-associated microbes like Akkermansia can worsen EAE. However, we have shown that Akkermansia strains isolated from subjects with MS can ameliorate disease, and studies from other groups have shown improvements in subjects with MS treated with propionate and in EAE mice treated with bile acids. We identified gut microbes that were correlated both with MRI and clinical measures of disease such as cognition and quality of life. Microbes from the genera Erysipelatoclostridium , Romboutsia , and Tyzzerella were positively correlated with a 2-year change in whole brain volume, indicating less atrophy in subjects with higher levels of these microbes. Erysipelatoclostridium has been associated with decreased lesion burden in pediatric subjects with MS. Romboutsia and members of the Peptostreptococcaceae family are reported to be elevated in MS and negatively correlated with healthy dietary interventions including the Mediterranean diet. Tyzzerella is elevated in pediatric MS, but has not been associated with disease worsening. We also found that a member of the Peptostreptococcaceae family positively correlated with a 2-year change in speed of processing as measured by SDMT, suggesting a beneficial role. Furthermore, members of the Blautia genus were negatively correlated with a 2-year worsening in Neuro-QoL domains, as was the Eubacterium hallii genus. Taken together, our data identify specific microbes with beneficial associations that are decreased in subjects with MS with disease progression. Clinical progression and microbiota composition in MS may be affected by DMT. To eliminate the confounder of treatment, we restricted our analyses to subjects who received the same treatment during the 2-year follow-up period. Furthermore, when we examined changes in worsening stratified by DMT, we found no differences in EDSS change, atrophy, or T2 lesion size. We did identify specific microbes that were altered in subjects treated with DMTs compared to untreated subjects. These included an increase in Blautia and a decrease in Bacteroides dorei in anti-CD20-treated subjects. To identify metabolites associated with MS progression, we performed global metabolomics on subjects with MS who transitioned from relapsing to progressive disease during the 2-year follow-up. Serum metabolites that were altered in stable vs. RR → SP subjects consisted of xenobiotics, lipids, and amino acids. Several serum metabolites were increased in subjects that transitioned to progressive MS, including palmitoleate, a lipid shown to be elevated in subjects with MS with an EDSS > 3, and p-cresol sulfate, a myelin basic protein mimic that has been shown to be elevated only in progressive MS. Secondary bile acids are modified by microbes and have important roles in health and disease. We found that two microbially derived bile acids in the serum, ursodeoxycholate and isoursodeoxycholate, were decreased in subjects who worsened. A decrease of these microbially derived bile acids suggests a potential beneficial role as demonstrated in mouse models. When we investigated stool metabolites, we found that most were decreased in subjects who progressed, including nicotinate (vitamin B3), nicotinate ribonucleoside, and protoporphyrin IX, which are cofactors/vitamins that have a beneficial role in the EAE mouse model of MS. The decrease in these beneficial metabolites in subjects who progressed could be explained by the production of nicotinate and other vitamin B metabolites by microbial taxa largely absent in these subjects, including Akkermansia. Altered sphingolipids have been detected in chronic MS lesions and are a target of therapy. We found that multiple sphingolipids were decreased in the stool of subjects who progressed. These included sphingosine and sphingomyelin, which are predicted to be made by multiple Lachnospiraceae including Eubacterium hallii . We identified numerous metabolites associated with stable disease that were predicted to be made by microbes that were downregulated in subjects with SPMS and RR → SP. Our study provides a comprehensive investigation of the microbiome and metabolome and how they are related to multiple measures of disease progression in MS over time. The use of longitudinal EDSS, brain MRI, and quality of life measures in a tightly controlled population enabled us to identify consistent beneficial associations with Blautia , Eubacterium , and Akkermansia and detrimental associations with Alistipes and Bacteroides across multiple measures of disease progression. In addition, we identified microbial metabolites in the serum and stool associated with the transition from relapsing to progressive MS. Taken together, our results identify an altered microbiota and metabolome in subjects with worsening disease and provide targets for the treatment of MS by modulation of the microbiome. Limitations of the study Our study presents important data on the impact of altered microbiota and metabolites on MS disease progression across 2 years; however, there are limitations. We included a relatively small number of study subjects ( Table S1 ), namely due to the demanding nature of the clinical and imaging studies that we performed. We were also limited by the use of 16S sequencing for microbial classification, and future work will benefit from similar longitudinal designs incorporating shotgun metagenomic methodologies. Taken together, our investigations provide testable targets for modifying the microbiome and its metabolites within the context of MS and identify the need for larger scale, longitudinal investigations that harness multi-site cohorts. STAR★Methods Key resources table Open in a new tab Experimental model and study participant details Subjects were originally recruited from the CLIMB study at the Brigham and Women’s Hospital MS center. Diagnosis of RRMS or Progressive MS, willingness to participate, and meeting the below inclusion and exclusion criteria were required for participation. All protocols were approved by the BWH institutional review board (IRB Protocol #: 2017P001169) and informed consent was obtained from every study subject. Inclusion criteria was a diagnosis of MS according to the latest McDonald criteria, with secondary and primary progressive MS being grouped together. Progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) was not quantified in these subjects. Exclusion criteria were current pregnancy, gastrointestinal surgical history, gastrointestinal disease, or antibiotics within 3 months prior to sample. Healthy control samples were garnered from healthy subjects from the PhenoGenetic Project, and processing procedures for these samples were identical to those from MS participants. After being enrolled, subjects were asked about their sex (male or female) but not gender (e.g., man, woman, nonbinary). Subjects who participated in SDMT, CVLT-II, or Neuro-QoL measurements underwent testing within 6 months of stool and blood donation. Subjects who transitioned from relapsing to progressive disease were classified according to their clinician’s diagnosis based on continued worsening of standard neurological exam measures and increasing EDSS. Subjects did not overlap between those included in Tables S1 and S3 . Dietary information was not collected at the time of sampling. Method details MRI methods People with MS in our CLIMB study undergo annual 3T MRI of the brain using a prescribed high-resolution protocol. We applied automated post-processing pipelines to measure T2LV, and whole brain and DGM volumes, after appropriate normalization. Volumetric data was collected within +/− 6 months of stool sample donation. Microbiome processing and analysis DNA was extracted from ∼200 mg stool using DNAeasy PowerLyzer Microbiome DNA extraction kits (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). The V4-5 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified per the updated Earth Microbiome Project’s barcoded primers. Paired-end sequencing was performed at the Harvard Biopolymers facility on a MiSeq and all samples were sequenced on the same run. Sequence analysis was done using QIIME2. Data was denoised and filtered using DADA2 and paired samples were subsequently merged. The table was filtered to remove samples from analysis that had less than 1,000 reads, appeared in only 1 sample, or were from known contaminate sequences. Taxonomic assignment was performed using a trained SILVA classifier that uses sequences from the November 2021 release of the SILVA rRNA database as a reference set. Statistical testing for α-diversity differences across disease subtype was done using a Kruskal-Wallis test, and β-diversity was analyzed by PERMANOVA with correction for multiple comparison testing. Species with less than 10% prevalence in any disease category were removed from statistical analyses. Viewing differences in composition across multi-variable samples, including longitudinal, age, EDSS, and disease status was performed in R using the Microbiome Multivariate Associations with Linear Models tool (MaAsLin2 ). MaAsLin2 analysis was performed while adjusting for the percentage of male and female subjects, age, and BMI. Spearman’s correlations between individual bacterial taxa linked with 3T MRI volumetric measures, cognitive tests, and Neuro-QoL domains were performed in R. Metabolomics Global metabolomics were performed by Metabolon Inc, (Durham, NC, USA) as previously described. Serum or stool samples, collected within +/− 45 days of each other and previously frozen at −80°C were processed with an 80% methanol extraction and metabolites detected via ultra-high performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Raw data was processed by Metabolon Inc, as described previously. Briefly, data was extracted from the mass spectrometer, quality-controlled, and aligned across individuals. Compounds were identified using an internal Metabolon library containing more than 5,400 purified standards. Samples were compared for retention times and mass/charge ratios to the purified standards. Retention time indices and mass spectral profiles were quality controlled to filter biochemicals with ranges outside of Metabolon’s database standards of +/− 10 parts/million of a library entry. For each identified metabolite, ion current area under the curve was used to generate raw abundances which were then log2-transformed and median-scaled by dividing the metabolite’s raw abundance by the median raw abundance of that metabolite across the entire dataset. Imputation for missing metabolites per sample was performed using the minimum median scaled abundance. For each metabolite, fold differences were determined between groups by dividing a metabolites average median scaled abundance in one group by another. Groupings contrasts were performed on diagnostic group (HC, RR → RR, RR → SP, or SP). Pathway enrichment scores (PES) were calculated to assess the overall contribution of a pathway to metabolite variance between diagnostic groups. PES were calculated using the following equation: Where “k” represents the number of metabolites reaching statistical significance in a given pathway, “m” is the total number of metabolites in said pathway, “n” is the total count of significant metabolites in all pathways, and “N” is all detected metabolites. A PES >1 was considered a contributor to group differences. GraphPad Prism Version 10.1.1 (San Diego, CA, USA) was used to visualize PES. Metabolite origins were ascertained using metOrigin and identified sources were plotted using Venn-diagrams. Microbial correlations with identified metabolites was performed using MMvec qiime2 plugin as previously described. SCFA quantification Stool samples were placed into a sterile Eppendorf tube prior to analysis of SCFAs via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry at the Massachusetts Host-Microbiome Center. Stool was weighed and between 0.1 and 0.4 g of stool was diluted in 1mL HPLC grade water prior to analysis for the following volatile acids: acetate, propionate, isobutyrate, butyrate, isovalerate, valerate, isocaproate, caproate, and heptanoate. Detectable levels were observed in a majority of samples for 6 SCFAs: acetate, propionate, butyrate, valerate, isobutyrate, and isovalerate. Values were normalized to the original input mass of stool sample prior to analysis. Bioinformatics tools Microbiome analyses were performed using Qiime2 (version 2023.5). R scripts were done in R (version 4.3.3) using R Studio (version 2023.12.1 + 402). MaAsLin2 was performed in R using a publicly available MaAsLin2 package (version 1.15.1) and controlled for covariates as described in pertinent experimental results. To control for situations where taxa were completely absent in one group but present in another, MaAsLin2 was adjusted to include a relative abundance pseudo-count of 0.0058, derived from the mean relative abundance when all zeroes were removed from the table. Spearman’s correlations were performed in R and Spearman’s rho and unadjusted p value are reported, except for CVLT-II analysis which were adjusted for age. MMvec (version 1.0.5) analysis on microbiota – metabolomic interactions was performed using a command line script in a Qiime2 environment (version 2020.6) and log conditional probabilities are reported. Quantification and statistical analysis Statistical analyses, except for specific bioinformatic tools, were performed using Prism 10 (Graphpad, v 10.2.2). All data where applicable are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM) and n -values represent number of subjects. Demographic comparisons (e.g., Figures 1 B and 1C) were done via Student’s t test without a Welch’s correction. Change in EDSS ( Figure 1 A) was analyzed via two-way ANOVA by time-point and disease category with a Sidak’s multiple comparison’s post-hoc test. Metabolomic analyses of variance were performed using a one-way ANCOVA to account for covariance factors in our dataset including age and BMI. For all metabolomic heatmaps, Log 2 (fold change) is reported with significance denoted by ANCOVA p -values when the false discovery statistic was q < 0.10. Metabolomic bar charts are expressions of batch normalized scaled intensity values for individual biochemicals, and significance annotations are based on ANCOVA results.
